title: The Educated Barbarian: Meditations analysis (part. 10)
summary: Part 10 of NH's Meditations reading (Book 5). He covers accepting fate without playing the victim, choosing imperfect action over perfectionism, the dangers of moral relativism, examining your own soul, guarding which impressions you let in, why humans are social, minimalism, and turning other people's hostility into fuel.
claims: Accepting fate means accepting that you have the power to change your situation; playing the victim of your circumstances is not acceptance
Endlessly asking what if I were taller or had better muscle-building genetics leaves you stuck and makes you dead weight to society; accept it and move on
Many would-be bodybuilders do nothing because they cannot get the perfect workout; between nothing and three push-ups, the correct choice is 30 push-ups, which lead to more
Action always beats thinking: if forced to choose between physical and mental, the physical produces more gains, and the mental is how you feed the fire intelligently
Being good at theory but worthless in practice is a trap that perfectionism leads to
Intelligence can manipulate concepts until they lose meaning; being able to never be wrong is dangerous and leads to moral relativism
Always know why you are thinking about something, or you will empty a concept of its meaning
You cannot calibrate your beliefs to society's, because most people never think about concepts or have been brainwashed; you might be happier but you would be stupider
Distrust yourself as an interpreter, since you are as unreliable as everyone else
Despair at the state of the world is not a reason to give up; stay true to yourself, because you are the one who lives with yourself
Being very busy can lead to dissociation, where you no longer fully recognise yourself in the mirror; people who go off the rails often forgot who they were
NH was happiest once his body matched his soul; his soul was never a skinny guy's, and reaching a satisfying level of muscularity made him far more confident and at home
The people around you shape your mind; parents must watch who their kids associate with, and adults are responsible for cutting negative influences, online and offline
Forced positivity and forced negativity are both harmful; negativity is a useful force, but emotions should be restrained to where they are useful
Wherever a man can live, he can live well; intelligence is partly the ability to adapt and flourish in more environments
A Stoic must live in society, because it is easy to be Stoic alone in a cave; the stimuli for your emotions almost always come from other people
NH is highly introverted but believes living entirely alone would be a life wasted
Humans also run on instinct, such as sexual drive, and animals can reason; humans are not better than animals, just smarter
People in their 20s should buy as little as possible; try a month without buying non-perishable goods, because possessions end up possessing you
Insults are requests for permission to hurt you; reject them and use the energy they create as fuel without engaging
